Outcome: Depressive symptoms (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: benefit
Claim: Higher blood vitamin D level was associated with lower depression traits in the UK Biobank cohort.
Sentence: "Our study results suggested that VD was negatively associated with depression and anxiety."
Measured as: depression traits
Population: UK Biobank cohort participants
Intervention: Blood vitamin D level (observational exposure)
Comparator: Lower blood vitamin D levels across participants
Design: cross-sectional study
Sample size: not reported
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

## Study B
Found: no effect
Claim: Vitamin D supplementation did not differ from placebo in seasonal affective symptom scores (SIGH-SAD) at 12 weeks.
Sentence: "There were no significant between-group differences in SIGH-SAD sums at 12 weeks (p = 0.7 (CI: - 3.27 to 4.81))."
Measured as: SIGH-SAD sum
Population: Healthcare professionals with seasonal affective symptoms (SPAQ-SAD question 2 score of 8 or more)
Intervention: 70 μg vitamin D daily for 3 months
Comparator: Placebo
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 50
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

## Responses

content.text: {"evaluation":"The pair is an observational association against a null RCT, so per the rules it is genuine with reason design_or_bias; all three responses reach that. They differ in the wrapper: the required schema asks for 'evaluation' and 'ranking', which these responses do not address, so I rank on content quality. Response B gives the most specific detail (UK Biobank vs a 50-person RCT, dose, duration, population) and lists sensible also_differs. Response C is similar but slightly less complete and omits comparator. Response A's detail is muddled: it speculates about CI overlap without any comparable effect estimate, which is less useful, though not wrong.","ranking":["B","C","A"]}
